paras: The shanghaiing of eight Black men from Savannah was the shipment of eight Black laborers from Savannah, Georgia, aboard the Russian bark Alice in July 1903 for a voyage to Bristol, England, where, by their account, they arrived beaten and were discharged unpaid. Harry Olsen, a Savannah sailor runner, and Jack Johnson, his Black runner, were arrested that September, and in April 1904 a federal jury convicted Olsen, who was sentenced to five years. Papers likened the practice to peonage, and the Savannah Morning News called it the first shanghaiing case brought under the federal kidnapping statute.

Olsen, also described as a shipping agent and boarding-house keeper, was already under bond for shipping two white youths, Joseph Terrell Rucker and John Seage, to Santos, Brazil, on the bark Kambira. The eight men were not seamen; Smallwood said they had only handled cotton on the levee and docks.

In affidavits sworn before Orin A. Lathrop, the American consul at Bristol, the men said Johnson offered them work loading lumber at Sapelo and took them down the river on a tug with Olsen in charge. According to the Sun's summary, they were made drunk on the way and, on reaching the Alice, told to board her or be put into the water. Smallwood said instead that he grew drowsy after drinks at a sailors' boarding house run by "a white man and a negro" and woke on a tug at sea. The bark's master, Captain Granit, gave Olsen $200 for the men, according to a receipt held by the district attorney.

The men said the Russian-speaking officers beat them for failing to understand orders, and that they worked the pumps of the leaking bark through a twenty-eight-day voyage. At Bristol they unloaded the cargo, were put off in a rowboat without pay, and were told they owed the captain $5 each.

Deputy marshals arrested Olsen and Johnson at Savannah on September 26, 1903, on eight warrants; Olsen gave a $1,600 bond and denied being a shanghaier, while Johnson stayed in jail for want of bond. The government had the men returned as witnesses, Smallwood by way of New York in October and others through Philadelphia. At a commissioner's hearing on November 18, the prosecution called none of the eight, and the crew of the tug McCauley testified that the men were sober and unthreatened.

A federal grand jury then indicted Olsen on four counts, including Smallwood and Easterlin, and also indicted Whitty McDonald, described as a Black man who had assisted him. On April 6, 1904, a jury in Judge Emory Speer's court found Olsen guilty of shanghaiing Smallwood, and the next day Speer imposed five years, the maximum, and a fine. Olsen was taken to the federal prison at Atlanta while his counsel prepared an appeal; no verdict for Johnson or McDonald was found.

A Savannah dispatch carried the arrests nationally under headlines such as "Seven Negroes Shanghaied" in the New York Sun, and a one-sentence digest item ran widely. The Savannah Morning News headlined the kidnapping of men "sold into servitude" while calling them a "double quartette of ebony-hued Americans," and a syndicated version ran as "Were Sold Into Slavery." The New York Evening World printed Smallwood's own story, later reprinted in Spokane.

Comparison with peonage recurred: the Sun called the method "worse than peonage in the interior of the State." Sentencing reports quoted Speer that "the most effective friend of the helpless and unprotected negro is the gentleman of the Southern communities." The only Black-press item found was the Richmond Planet's reprint of the digest sentence on October 3, 1903, without comment.

The men's accounts of liquor, deception and threats, including labor "at the point of a pistol," were contradicted at the November hearing by the tug's crew and Olsen, though the trial jury credited the men. John Gilliard, apparently the James Gillard of the first list, said he had boarded the Alice only to deliver potatoes. Reports also differ on the date (July 1 or July 9), the number of men (seven or eight), the payment ($200 or $250) and the fine ($5,000 or $300).

reader.title: Shanghaiing of eight Black men from Savannah
bases: Eight Black laborers were, by their sworn accounts, taken aboard a ship against their will, sold to its master for $200 and made to work the voyage unpaid under beatings, which the papers called 'servitude' and likened to peonage (A3, A4, A19, A20).

The men's affidavits (A3, A4), Smallwood's separate accounts (A10, A12), the receipt and the April 1904 jury verdict (A20, A21) agree on the core event, though defense witnesses at the November hearing denied force (A17).

accounts.label: The men's affidavits
accounts.gist: Johnson offered them work loading lumber at Sapelo; on the tug they were made drunk and told to board the Alice or swim; they were beaten at sea and discharged at Bristol owing the master $5 each.

accounts.label: Moses Smallwood
accounts.gist: He was drugged with drinks at a sailors' boarding house run by a white man and a Black man, woke on a tug, fought the second officer, and was beaten daily on the 28-day voyage.

accounts.label: John Gilliard
accounts.gist: A farmer, he went aboard the Alice to deliver potatoes and was kept aboard when she sailed.

accounts.label: Defense witnesses and Olsen
accounts.gist: The tug's captain and mate said the men were sober, unthreatened and objected only to the ship's rig; Olsen said he was paid $10 a man and used no force.

accounts.label: Trial witnesses and jury
accounts.gist: Witnesses testified Olsen held them aboard against their will and that they were whipped at sea; the jury found Olsen guilty.

framing.detail: The Savannah Morning News headlined the kidnapping of men 'sold into servitude' and called the practice akin to peonage, while describing the men as a 'double quartette of ebony-hued Americans'.
Wire and syndicate versions ran as 'Seven Negroes Shanghaied', 'Arrested for Shanghai Negroes' and 'Were Sold Into Slavery'.
The New York Evening World ran Smallwood's account as 'an amazing story of kidnapping' with the deck 'All Cruelly Beaten'.
Sentencing reports headlined the 'limit of law' and quoted Speer calling Southern gentlemen 'the most effective friend of the helpless and unprotected negro'.
The Richmond Planet carried only the one-sentence digest item, without comment.

info: Men taken from Savannah in early July 1903: July 1 (Smallwood, boarding house), 'the first week in July' (Smallwood in New York), or July 9 (affidavit as given by the Sun).
Recruited at Savannah, Ga.; carried down the river by tug and put aboard the Russian bark Alice at Sapelo (A4, A7, A17) or on the way to Tybee Road (A3); landed at Bristol, England.

Eight Savannah Black men: John Porter, Joe Easterlin, Jesse Hall, William Jones, James Gillard, Ben Manigault, Moses Smallwood and Benty Washington; 'nearly all of them are young boys' (A4). The Sun says seven.

Harry Olsen (Oleson), a sailor runner, shipping agent and sailors' boarding-house keeper, and Jack (Jake) Johnson, a Black runner working for him; the bark's officers beat the men at sea; Whitty McDonald, a Black man, later indicted as an assistant.

Olsen sentenced April 7, 1904 to five years, the maximum, and a fine ($5,000 in A22 and A23; $300 in A25); taken to the Atlanta federal prison; counsel announced an appeal. No outcome for Johnson or McDonald was found.
